analysis.tldr: A massive flood of money into Indian banks is driving up worries about inflation (rising prices of everyday goods), which means the central bank may make borrowing more expensive.
the_story: India received a record $133 billion in diaspora inflows (money sent home by Indians living abroad).
This huge inflow flooded banks with extra cash, pushing overnight interest rates below the Reserve Bank of India's (RBI) 5.25% policy rate.
The Reserve Bank of India (RBI, India's central bank) has already drained more than ₹1 trillion (one lakh crore rupees) from the banking system.
Food and oil prices are fueling inflation concerns, and markets are now pricing in a possible RBI interest-rate hike.
analysis.what_happened: A record $133 billion came into India from overseas workers and families. This huge amount of money flooded the banking system with excess cash, making short-term interest rates drop below the central bank's target rate. Because this extra money risks pushing up prices (inflation)—already stoked by food and oil costs—the central bank has sucked out over ₹1 trillion, and markets now expect it to raise interest rates.
analysis.analogy: It is like a local market suddenly getting flooded with too much cash; people start buying things faster, shopkeepers raise their prices, and the village elders have to step in to lock up some of that cash so things don't get too expensive.
why_it_matters_india: Diaspora money floods Indian banks with excess cash, dropping overnight interest rates below the RBI's policy rate.
Excess cash in the system threatens to drive up inflation (rising prices of everyday goods) alongside existing food and oil cost pressures.
The RBI reacts by draining over ₹1 trillion out of the banking system to control this extra money.
Markets expect the RBI to turn hawkish (favoring higher interest rates to fight inflation), raising borrowing costs for everyone.

impacts.target: Loan interest rates (home, car, and personal loans)
impacts.rationale: If the RBI raises interest rates to fight inflation, banks will make loans costlier — generally bad for borrowers paying EMIs.
Sucking cash out of the system and potentially raising rates aims to cool down rising prices, which is good for household budgets.

impacts.target: 10-year bond yield (interest India pays to borrow)
impacts.rationale: As markets expect tighter money and rate hikes, bond yields tend to rise — making government borrowing more expensive.

watch_next: Future announcements from the Reserve Bank of India on draining more cash from banks
Upcoming inflation data tracking food and oil prices
analysis.caveats: Global oil and food prices could shift unexpectedly, changing the inflation pressure that drives the central bank's next moves.

events.article_text:
Trump Admits Diesel U.S. Export Ban Could Raise Gasoline Prices

What I Cover Tsvetana Paraskova is an energy and commodities journalist who has contributed to Oilprice.com for nearly a decade, covering global energy markets, commodities,…

A potential ban on U.S. diesel exports could have “a negative impact on gasoline,” U.S. President Donald Trump said late on Wednesday, although he didn’t rule out such a move from the Administration.

The President told reporters in the Oval Office that he and the Administration continue to discuss the pros and cons of a diesel export ban every day, “but it just seems that it would have a negative impact on gasoline.”

Earlier this week, Goldman Sachs analysts also warned that a U.S. diesel export ban would push domestic gasoline prices higher as refiners could be forced to reduce processing rates.

President Trump on Wednesday appeared to be less inclined to ban diesel exports than a few days ago, but he has not yet ruled out the idea that emerged last month as retail diesel prices in the United States hit $6 per gallon nationwide average for the first time ever, and then $6.50 a gallon.

As a result of the jump in crude oil prices and a worsening global crunch for fuels, U.S. gasoline prices are also at a record high level for this time of year, even as demand is easing after the end of the peak driving season. At an average nationwide price of $4.43 per gallon, the price of regular gasoline is higher than the $4.08 from a month ago and way higher than $3.15 per gallon on this day in 2025.

Diesel prices have hit record highs in many economies amid refinery constraints in the Middle East and Russia, which refineries elsewhere cannot offset even if they run at maximum utilization rates, as is the case in the United States.

Refinery capacity is constrained in the Middle East due to Iranian strikes on refineries and the trickle of fuel flows through the Strait of Hormuz. Then there is also severely restricted capacity in Russia due to Ukrainian drone strikes at Russian refineries. Russia has just extended its ban on diesel exports through October 31.

analysis.tldr: If the US bans diesel exports, it could push global fuel prices even higher, eventually making petrol and diesel costlier for everyday Indians.
the_story: U.S. President Donald Trump stated that a potential ban on U.S. diesel exports could have a negative impact on gasoline.
The idea of a diesel ban emerged after U.S. retail diesel prices hit record highs of $6 and then $6.50 per gallon nationwide.
Goldman Sachs analysts warned that a diesel export ban would push U.S. gasoline prices higher because oil refiners might have to reduce processing rates.

Global fuel prices are already climbing due to refinery constraints, including Iranian strikes in the Middle East, a trickle of fuel through the Strait of Hormuz, and Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian refineries.
U.S. regular gasoline prices reached a record $4.43 per gallon on the day of reporting, up from $4.08 a month ago and $3.15 a year ago.
analysis.what_happened: U.S. President Donald Trump admitted that banning U.S. diesel exports could hurt gasoline prices, though his administration is still discussing the idea. The proposal was initially considered because retail diesel prices in the US surged to record levels. However, experts and the President warn that restricting diesel from leaving the country could accidentally force oil refineries to slow down, making other fuels like gasoline even more expensive.
analysis.analogy: It is like a local bakery that makes both bread and biscuits; if you force them to stop selling biscuits to neighboring towns, their whole kitchen might get clogged up, making bread harder to bake and more expensive for everyone.
why_it_matters_india: Global crude oil and fuel markets are deeply interconnected, so supply issues and export bans in major economies like the US ripple across the world.
If global fuel prices rise due to U.S. export restrictions and Middle Eastern and Russian supply disruptions, it becomes costlier for India to import crude oil.
Higher import costs for oil force local oil companies to pay more to buy and process crude.
Ultimately, this can translate to higher retail prices for petrol and diesel in India, increasing transport costs and overall inflation (general rise in prices of goods).

impacts.rationale: higher global fuel prices and refinery bottlenecks drive up import costs for India, which is bad for everyday consumers who pay more at the pump.
costlier transport fuel makes moving goods more expensive, raising prices for everyday household items — bad for consumers.
higher oil import bills mean India needs more US dollars to buy fuel, which can weaken the rupee (each rupee buys fewer dollars) — generally bad for importers.

watch_next: Whether the U.S. administration actually moves forward with a ban on diesel exports
Updates on fuel flows through the Strait of Hormuz and refinery statuses in the Middle East and Russia
analysis.caveats: President Trump's stance could shift rapidly, and if the U.S. decides against an export ban, the immediate upward pressure on global fuel prices might ease.

events.headline: Writing the Playbook: A Strategy and Doctrine for American Economic Security

items.title: Writing the Playbook: A Strategy and Doctrine for American Economic Security
items.summary: In January, this article series opened with a blunt question: Economic statecraft is back, but is America ready?Driving the question, in part, was the fact that the United States had not yet articulated (at least overtly) a strategy for economic statecraft. This was despite widening recognition that nations were increasingly using economic tools like tariffs and sanctions to pursue strategic objectives. U.S. awareness was particularly elevated by the realization during COVID-19 that decades of Chinese market manipulation, predatory trade behaviors, and security vulnerabilities deployed against

events.article_text:
Driving the question, in part, was the fact that the United States had not yet articulated (at least overtly) a strategy for economic statecraft. This was despite widening recognition that nations were increasingly using economic tools like tariffs and sanctions to pursue strategic objectives. U.S. awareness was particularly elevated by the realization during COVID-19 that decades of Chinese market manipulation, predatory trade behaviors, and security vulnerabilities deployed against its markets had gone unanswered.

On the eve of the nation’s 250th anniversary, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent fired a shot across the bow. He announced a framework for economic statecraft driven by “the disciplined use of America’s economic power in service of our sovereignty,” embracing Alexander Hamilton’s principle that every nation “ought to endeavor to possess within itself all the essentials of national supply.” The strategy, which Bessent delivered to the Economic Club of New York and outlined publicly in the Wall Street Journal, centered on five principles: economic security begins with national capacity; American openness will be matched by reciprocity; America will write the rules of the next economy; financial leadership is a central instrument of statecraft; and economic statecraft should serve the American people.

Bessent’s five principles are generally an amalgamation of bipartisan economic statecraft concepts pursued since at least 2011 (albeit a departure from 80-plus years of post-war, Bretton Woods-framed geoeconomics). They also underscore the difficulty of crafting a comprehensive economic strategy given very real tradeoffs between America’s economic exceptionalism and its national security goals. Tensions among the strategy’s principles are evident. For example, economic security derived from national capacity harkens to autarky, but American openness enabled by reciprocity points toward conditional engagement in an international trading system.

Despite its unproven state, Bessent and the executive branch have framed an overdue and much-needed strategy for economic statecraft. While the speech was a clarifying point for planners at Treasury, Commerce, the State Department, the Combatant Commands, and other agencies, the doctrine to follow — the guide for the strategy’s implementation — is yet to be developed and should be adopted in concert with ongoing practices and guidance, while holding true to national values, institutional norms, and an independent private sector. That will require engagement with lawmakers, industry, and academics to reconcile tensions, and so practitioners are productively mobilized to realize the strategy’s vision. While current efforts across the executive and legislative branches, industry, academia, and policy communities can serve as helpful guides, they are generally siloed and uncoordinated. Success therefore demands that doctrine be developed and orchestrated collaboratively across these communities.

Enabling elements include designating a “referee” for economic statecraft in the executive branch, a settled “home” for it in Congress, paradigm-shifting incentives for industry to partner with government, workforce investment, and evolution in academia. While many tradeoffs remain unresolved, these and future policy solutions will help leaders recognize and accept the risks required for meaningful change.

Bessent’s speech is the most senior entry in a rapid buildup of economic security policy activities across the executive branch this year.

In April, the Pentagon’s Deputy Secretary of Defense Stephen Feinberg formally established the Economic Defense Unit, a hub charged with fusing economic leverage and requirements into joint military planning and operations by developing requirements for economic competition activities. It joins the Office of Strategic Capital in a growing Pentagon ecosystem focused on gaining strategic advantage via economic leverage.

The analytic foundation for that pursuit is also underway. The Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency’s National Security Economic Theory program aims to put geoeconomics on a more quantitative and rigorous theoretical footing. A companion effort, the Anticipatory and Adaptive Anti-Money Laundering program, targets the machinery of illicit finance. For a discipline that lacks objective metrics and testable models due to its nascency, wargaming geoeconomics with rigor and intentionality is a necessity to build confidence in practice, policy, and process.

The work ahead requires putting the strategy on paper so bureaucracies can consider and ingest it into process and practice. Bureaucrats thrive on regulatory guidance, as it is their impetus for action or inaction (and thus Congressional oversight). Bessent’s five principles deserve similar treatment to what the National Defense Strategy does for the military instrument: a published economic security strategy nested within the national security strategy, with interagency doctrine and campaign plans following in turn.

Ongoing doctrinal work is ripe for adoption and then operationalization but it should be synchronized. The core task requires integrating economic considerations into both joint planning and the combatant commands, where commanders hold the day-to-day partner relationships upon which multilateral pressure campaigns depend. Success will require building requisite playbooks and wargames to give Washington options when a crisis arrives. To execute, the executive branch should establish an entity akin to the Economic Warfare Operations Capability with definitive authority to prioritize and act on offensive and defensive economic statecraft decisions. It should be informed by a joint public-private fused intelligence and analytics enterprise, in conjunction with domestic and foreign industry partners.

analysis.tldr: A major shift in U.S. economic strategy toward tighter trade controls could ripple through global supply chains, affecting Indian export opportunities and foreign investment flows.
the_story: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced a new framework for U.S. economic statecraft at the Economic Club of New York, centered on five principles including national capacity and reciprocity.
The framework moves away from decades of post-war global trading norms, reacting to what the U.S. views as Chinese market manipulation and trade vulnerabilities exposed during COVID-19.
The Pentagon has established new bodies like the Economic Defense Unit and research programs to fuse economic leverage into military planning and counter illicit finance.
The strategy remains an unproven framework that will require detailed doctrine, legislative backing, and coordination between government, industry, and academia.
analysis.what_happened: U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent introduced a formal strategy for American economic statecraft, aiming to use tools like tariffs and financial power more aggressively to protect U.S. sovereignty. This follows years of growing U.S. awareness of security vulnerabilities and trade practices from competitors like China.
analysis.analogy: It is like a local grocery shop owner deciding to stop buying goods exclusively from a single giant supplier who undercut everyone, and instead building a secure backyard greenhouse while demanding strict trade rules from all other partners.
why_it_matters_india: The U.S. pushes for domestic industrial capacity and strict trade reciprocity -> Global supply chains reshuffle further away from traditional manufacturing hubs -> Indian manufacturing and exporters navigate changing U.S. trade rules ('China+1' diversification trends).

U.S. agencies ramp up economic defense and financial tracking -> Global compliance and screening requirements tighten -> Multinational firms doing business with both the U.S. and emerging markets face stricter regulatory hurdles.

U.S. shifts toward aggressive economic statecraft -> Global market sentiment reacts to shifting trade policies -> Foreign institutional investors adjust risk allocations across emerging markets including India.

impacts.rationale: Broader global trade tensions or supply chain uncertainties created by aggressive U.S. policies can trigger caution among foreign investors, which is generally bad for domestic stock momentum.

If U.S. policy shifts focus heavily inward toward domestic capacity and stricter economic controls, corporate spending by American clients could slow down, which is unfavorable for Indian tech exporters.

watch_next: Specific legislative proposals or tariffs introduced by the U.S. Treasury and Congress following Bessent's framework
Further coordination between the Pentagon's Economic Defense Unit and commercial industry partners
analysis.caveats: The article outlines a high-level strategic speech and bureaucratic plans rather than immediate, enacted trade laws or tariffs.

analysis.tldr: When big foreign investors pull massive amounts of money out of India, stock market indices like the Nifty and Sensex go down, which can dent the value of your mutual funds and investments.
the_story: Foreign institutional investors (big international investment funds) pulled out over Rs 20,000 crore from Indian equities in just two trading sessions.
The Nifty and Sensex (India's main stock market indices) are heading for an eighth straight weekly decline.
Elevated crude (raw oil) prices, high US bond yields (interest rates paid by the US government), and rate concerns have weighed heavily on market sentiment.
analysis.what_happened: International investment funds pulled over Rs 20,000 crore out of the Indian stock market in just two days. This massive selling happened because high crude oil prices, rising interest rates in the US, and worries about future interest rate cuts made global investors nervous, causing them to take their money out of emerging markets like India.
analysis.analogy: It is like a group of wealthy guests suddenly deciding to pack up and leave a party because they heard a rumor that a better party with free snacks is starting down the street, causing the main dance floor to empty out.
why_it_matters_india: Global investors sell Indian shares to move their money to safer or higher-paying options abroad, like US bonds.
Heavy selling causes the Nifty and Sensex to drop for the eighth week in a row.
As stock prices fall, the value of everyday mutual funds and retirement portfolios holding these shares temporarily goes down.
This capital flight can also put pressure on the rupee (Indian currency) as dollars are pulled out of the country.

impacts.rationale: Massive selling by foreign investors pushes overall stock prices down, which can make your stock portfolio look smaller in the short term.
When foreign investors pull money out, they convert rupees back into dollars, which can weaken the rupee and make imported items like electronics and crude oil more expensive.

watch_next: Whether foreign investors continue selling or slow down their pullout
Movements in US bond yields and global crude oil prices
analysis.caveats: If global sentiment shifts or US inflation data improves, foreign investors could suddenly reverse course and start buying back into Indian stocks.

events.headline: Indian Cabinet approves 1-10% hike in rabi crops minimum support price

items.title: Indian Cabinet approves 1-10% hike in rabi crops minimum support price
items.summary: MSP for wheat now stands at ₹2,610 per quintal against ₹2,585 per quintal announced for 2026-27 marketing season (April-March)

events.article_text:
Total payout to farmers is estimated to be ₹90,962 crore for 324 lakh tonnes in the 2027-28 marketing year.

The Indian government announced minimum support prices (MSPs) for the rabi marketing season 2027-28 after the Cabinet approved 1-10 per cent hike on Wednesday, a day before the winter sowing season is set to commence. The lowest hike in wheat was less than 1 per cent while the highest was for safflower by 10.3 per cent.

After the revision, the MSP of winter season’s main cereal wheat now stands at ₹2,610 per quintal against ₹2,585 per quintal announced for 2026-27 marketing season (April-March).

India may get normal rain during Oct-Dec as S-W monsoon ends with 14th lowest rainfall in 125 years

Briefing media after the Cabinet meeting, Information and Broadcasting Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw said that the Cabinet approved the MSPs recommendations of the Commission for Agricultural Costs and Prices (CACP) as proposed by the agriculture ministry.

“The production cost of wheat is ₹1,264 per quintal, but MSP has been kept more than double at ₹2,610 per quintal for 2027-28,” he said.

Among other rabi crops, barley MSP has been increased by 6.3 per cent to ₹2,286 per quintal from ₹2,150 per quintal, gram (chana) has been hiked by 1.4 per cent to ₹5,958 per quintal from ₹5,875 per quintal, lentil (masur) by 5.6 per cent to ₹7,390 per quintal from ₹7,000 per quintal, mustard by 6.7 per cent to ₹6,613 per quintal from ₹6,200 per quintal and safflower to ₹7,215 per quintal from ₹6,540 per quintal, an official statement said.

The government has fixed a production target of 177.72 million tonnes (mt) of foodgrains which includes 121 mt of wheat, 17.20 mt of pulses and 22.30 mt of nutri/coarse cereals during current rabi season. As the monsoon rainfall during whole of September was only 8 per cent deficient, some parts may be able to have adequate moisture for sowing.

However, some states which have received 20 per cent or more deficit rainfall in September may have to depend entirely for canal irrigation amid forecast of further strengthening of El Nino in the coming months. During September, Maharashtra reported 52 per cent deficit rainfall, Karnataka -57 per cent, Telangana -24 per cent, Punjab -64 per cent and Haryana -44 per cent.

Satyam Shivam Sundaram, Partner, Strategy & Transactions, EY LLP, said the higher MSP increases for oilseeds and pulses, coupled with a relatively modest increase for wheat, reflect a calibrated policy shift towards crop diversification, import substitution, and a broader move from a food security centric approach towards nutrition security.

“The stronger incentives for crops such as rapeseed-mustard, safflower and masur are well aligned with India’s long-term objective of enhancing self-sufficiency in edible oils and pulses, reducing import dependence, and strengthening farm income resilience,” he said.

However, MSP is only one part of the equation. Meaningful and sustained shifts in cropping patterns will occur only when farmers have confidence in assured procurement, market access, value-chain linkages, and supporting investments in storage, processing and logistics, Sundaram said.

“The announcement should, therefore, be viewed as an important step within a broader agricultural transformation agenda rather than a standalone pricing intervention. Sustained procurement and value chain support will ultimately be critical to translating these policy signals into on-ground acreage diversification and long-term farmer prosperity,” he said.

analysis.tldr: Higher assured prices for winter crops mean better earnings for farmers, but could also push up food prices for everyday shoppers.
the_story: The Indian Cabinet approved a 1 to 10 percent hike in minimum support prices [MSP, the guaranteed floor price paid by the government to farmers] for rabi [winter-sown] crops for the 2027-28 marketing year.
The MSP for wheat rose slightly by less than 1 percent to ₹2,610 per quintal, while safflower saw the highest jump of 10.3 percent to ₹7,215 per quintal.
The total estimated payout to farmers is ₹90,962 crore for 324 lakh tonnes of crops.
Experts note the higher hikes for oilseeds and pulses reflect a policy shift toward encouraging crop diversification and nutrition security.
analysis.what_happened: The government raised the guaranteed minimum prices it pays farmers for winter crops right before the sowing season begins. This decision follows recommendations from the Commission for Agricultural Costs and Prices and aims to encourage farmers to grow more pulses and oilseeds.
analysis.analogy: It is like a company setting a guaranteed minimum bonus for its workers to encourage them to make different types of products next season.
why_it_matters_india: The government raises MSPs for winter crops by 1 to 10 percent.
Farmers receive higher guaranteed payouts, totaling ₹90,962 crore.
Higher procurement costs can increase government spending and stoke food inflation [the rate at which the cost of food items increases].
Consumers face potentially higher prices for daily food items like pulses and edible oils in retail markets.

impacts.rationale: higher support prices can raise overall food prices, which is bad for household budgets as daily expenses go up.
costlier raw farm ingredients can squeeze profit margins for packaged food companies, which is generally bad for stock performance.

watch_next: Actual farmer planting choices for wheat versus pulses and oilseeds
Rainfall and reservoir levels in states with deficient September rainfall like Punjab and Maharashtra
analysis.caveats: Actual crop production and market prices will depend heavily on weather conditions and water availability during the winter sowing season.

analysis.tldr: New RBI rules for international credit card payments could make buying foreign services harder and add paperwork for consumers.
the_story: New regulations from the Reserve Bank of India (RBI, India's central banking institution) will mandate reporting of international credit card transactions starting October 1.
Consumers may need to provide details on all payments for services purchased abroad, such as subscriptions for Claude, The New Yorker, and Bandcamp.
The existing framework lacks clarity on how individuals will actually report these transactions to banks.

While international credit card purchases fall under the Liberalised Remittance Scheme (a scheme allowing resident individuals to freely remit a certain amount abroad), the specific reporting process remains unclear.
analysis.what_happened: The Reserve Bank of India introduced a new mandate starting October 1 that requires reporting for international credit card transactions. This happened because authorities want tighter tracking of money flowing out of India for foreign services. However, the current rules do not clearly explain how regular people are supposed to report these details to their banks.
analysis.analogy: It is like your apartment building suddenly asking you to fill out a form for every single food delivery you order from outside the neighborhood, but nobody has told you where to pick up the form or who to hand it to.
why_it_matters_india: The RBI introduces new compliance rules starting October 1 -> consumers face extra paperwork for international card payments.
Lack of clear reporting guidelines -> confusion for users trying to pay for foreign digital services and subscriptions.
Transactions tied to the Liberalised Remittance Scheme -> greater scrutiny on how money leaves India for personal services abroad.

impacts.target: Ease of digital subscriptions and foreign services
impacts.rationale: Extra compliance steps and reporting hurdles will make paying for overseas digital services more annoying for regular users.

watch_next: Clearer guidelines from banks on how to report international card transactions before October 1
Updates from popular foreign subscription services regarding Indian payment methods
analysis.caveats: The text contains mostly headline snippets alongside the main article, so implementation details could shift if the RBI issues clarifying circulars.

events.headline: WTO members deepen discussions on trade and climate measures, share updates

items.title: WTO members deepen discussions on trade and climate measures, share updates
items.summary: The Committee on Trade and Environment (CTE) met on 28-29 September to advance its discussions on the trade and environment nexus, focusing on interoperability and development aspects of trade-related climate measures. Members also built on the voluntary information sharing exercise launched earlier this year with a view to enhancing transparency of trade and climate measures in the Committee. In addition, they were briefed on work undertaken in other international fora and on developments in several member-led environmental initiatives at the WTO.

events.article_text:
This note has been prepared by the WTO Secretariat to assist public understanding about the work of the WTO's councils, committees and other bodies. It is not intended as a complete account of all issues raised at the meeting. These can be found in the formal meeting minutes.

The Chair of the CTE, Ambassador Ram Prasad Subedi of Nepal, facilitated the regular meeting on 29 September, which was preceded by a thematic session on 28 September.

The CTE's thematic session on "trade-related climate measures, including interoperability and development aspects" was co-moderated by Mr Håvard Hugås of Norway and Ms Nur Karabag of Türkiye.

The session sought to move the discussions beyond a general mapping of trade-related climate measures (TrCMs) towards a more operational examination of what interoperability means in practice. The discussion sought to identify where compliance challenges arise for governments and businesses, with a focus on steel, while exploring cooperative solutions and integrating development considerations in regulatory design choices, implementation, and monitoring, reporting and verification (MRV) systems.

Through expert panel discussions, the session examined the issues and discussed tools, mechanisms and frameworks that could address compliance challenges and increase cooperation, including at the WTO.

The subsequent discussion among members reinforced these themes. Australia and China circulated an informal, non-official document for discussion, putting forward some ideas on interoperability and possible follow-up in the CTE.

Since November 2023, the CTE has held thematic and interactive sessions on topics of interest to the membership. Previous sessions have addressed topics such as the clean energy transition, sustainable agriculture, trade-related climate measures, and technology transfer.

All presentations delivered at this seventh thematic session are available here.

Based on the CTE Chair's proposal, the next CTE thematic session will be held in December 2026 with a focus on environmental goods and services, including bio-inputs. This will be followed by a session on the circular economy in February 2027. Co-moderators will help shape these sessions.

Members heard an update from co-sponsors on a joint submission, titled "Non-binding Guidance on Measures Requiring Measurement of Emissions of Goods Traded Across Borders," submitted by Australia, Canada, Chile, Costa Rica, Israel, Japan, the Republic of Korea, New Zealand and the United Kingdom (WT/CTE/W/269/Rev.6).

Co-sponsors emphasized the importance of enhancing transparency and fostering a shared understanding of good practices and methodologies for measuring embedded carbon emissions in traded goods.

The United Kingdom shared information on its "UK Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (UK CBAM): Monitoring, Reporting and Verification" (WT/CTE/INF/9). The UK CBAM is scheduled to enter into force on 1 January 2027.

The information was shared on a voluntary basis using the standardized template in document WT/CTE/W/271. At the June CTE meeting, Japan and Australia became the first two members to use the template to share information of their domestic trade-related climate measures (TrCMs).

Members welcomed the UK's submission as a practical means of enhancing transparency in the Committee. Many sought clarifications or further information while others expressed concerns about the measure's potential impact on market access and the compliance burdens it could impose on developing and least-developed countries, as well as small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). Colombia also provided an oral update on its own measure.

Members were briefed by the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) Secretariat on preparations for the upcoming Climate Change Conference (COP31), to be held in Antalya, Türkiye, in November 2026. The COP31 Presidency (Türkiye) also updated members on plans for the conference, including a Finance and Trade Day scheduled for 13 November. The WTO Secretariat reported on its preparations and participation at COP31.

The Secretariat of the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) presented recent developments and preparations for the CBD's 17th Conference of the Parties (COP17), to be held in Yerevan, Armenia, in October 2026. The delegation of Armenia, as hosts of COP17, supplemented this briefing, highlighting its priorities and seeking members' active engagement at COP17.

The Secretariat of the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES) briefed members on recent developments and main outcomes from the CITES' 20th Conference of the Parties (COP20), that was held in Samarkand, Uzbekistan, from 24 November to 5 December 2025.

The CTE was briefed by the co-sponsors of the member-led Dialogue on Plastics Pollution and Environmentally Sustainable Plastics Trade (DPP), the Trade and Environmental Sustainability Structured Discussions (TESSD) and the Fossil Fuels Subsidy Reform (FFSR) initiative on their recent activities and planned work.

The WTO Secretariat also presented an update on the WTO Environmental Database (EDB).

The next meeting of the Committee is scheduled for 4-5 February 2027.

analysis.tldr: New global green trade rules and carbon taxes could soon make it costlier for Indian manufacturing exporters to sell goods like steel abroad.
the_story: The WTO's Committee on Trade and Environment (CTE), chaired by Ambassador Ram Prasad Subedi of Nepal, held a meeting on 29 September preceded by a thematic session on 28 September.
The United Kingdom shared information on its UK Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (UK CBAM) monitoring and reporting system, which is scheduled to enter into force on 1 January 2027.
Developing countries and small businesses expressed concerns during the meetings about potential negative impacts on market access and heavy compliance burdens.
Countries including Australia, Canada, Chile, Costa Rica, Israel, Japan, South Korea, New Zealand, and the UK updated members on joint guidelines for measuring carbon emissions in traded goods.
analysis.what_happened: Countries at the World Trade Organization (WTO — an international organization that sets rules for global trade) gathered to discuss how environmental rules and climate measures affect international commerce. Specifically, nations discussed carbon taxes on imported goods and how to measure greenhouse gas emissions without creating unfair hurdles for developing nations.
analysis.analogy: It is like a society of shopkeepers trying to agree on a universal rule that every item sold must carry a label showing how much electricity was used to make it, so customers can judge its carbon footprint.
why_it_matters_india: Global trade bodies are pushing forward with carbon measurement rules and border taxes like the UK's upcoming CBAM in January 2027.
Indian manufacturing exporters, particularly in carbon-heavy sectors like steel, face upcoming compliance hurdles and extra reporting costs.
Higher compliance and tax costs can erode profit margins for Indian exporters competing in Western markets.
This increases overall pressure on Indian industrial exporters to adopt greener production methods to maintain market access.

impacts.rationale: New reporting rules and carbon border taxes like the UK CBAM could increase costs and hurt competitiveness for Indian companies selling abroad — generally bad for exporters.
Increased regulatory burdens on heavy industries could slightly weigh on sentiment for metal and manufacturing stocks, which is generally unfavorable for the broader market.

watch_next: The implementation and rules of the UK Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism ahead of January 2027
Further updates from the WTO Committee on Trade and Environment meetings scheduled for February 2027
analysis.caveats: The WTO discussions are currently focused on sharing information and transparency, meaning mandatory global enforcement rules are still evolving and subject to change.

events.headline: Best of BS Opinion: RBI's currency intervention must be limited

items.title: Best of BS Opinion: RBI's currency intervention must be limited
items.summary: From RBI intervention in the rupee and questions over electoral-roll revisions to distressed assets, India's growth challenges and political grief, today's opinions examine institutional and economic

analysis.tldr: Opinions suggest the RBI (Reserve Bank of India [India's central bank that controls money and interest rates]) should cut back on its heavy buying and selling of foreign currencies, which can affect the value of our money and market stability.
the_story: A Business Standard opinion piece argues that the RBI's currency intervention (buying or selling foreign money to control the rupee's exchange rate) must be limited.
Only the headline was available for this analysis.
analysis.what_happened: The Business Standard newspaper published an opinion article suggesting that the central bank should restrict its active steps in the currency market. This happens when experts debate how much the government should try to control the price of the rupee (the Indian currency) against foreign money like the US dollar.
analysis.analogy: It is like a parent constantly stepping in to keep a seesaw perfectly balanced instead of letting the children figure out how to ride it on their own.
why_it_matters_india: The RBI steps into the currency market to stop the rupee from swinging too wildly up or down.
If the central bank reduces this intervention, the rupee might start moving more freely based on global supply and demand.
A freely moving currency can make imported items like crude oil more expensive or cheaper, feeding into overall inflation (rising prices of everyday goods).
Regular people should care because how the RBI manages our currency affects everything from the cost of foreign travel to imported fuel prices.

impacts.rationale: Without heavy central bank intervention, the currency could see more natural ups and downs, which can sometimes make imports costlier and pinch household budgets.
If a less-managed currency causes imported goods like oil to become pricier, it generally leads to higher inflation—bad news for everyday buyers.

watch_next: Official statements or policy changes from the RBI regarding its foreign exchange reserves management
Further opinion pieces and editorials discussing the future of Indian currency controls
analysis.caveats: Only the headline was available, so specific details, arguments, and data from the actual article text are missing.

events.headline: Playing both sides of the U.S.-China AI “Cold War”

items.title: Playing both sides of the U.S.-China AI “Cold War”
items.summary: From Latin America to Southeast Asia, countries are dividing their AI investments between the two superpowers rather than choosing one over the other.

events.article_text:
Saudi Arabia celebrated the launch of what it calls the world’s most advanced Arabic-language AI model earlier this month. The technology behind it came from China even as the kingdom spends billions building its AI infrastructure with American companies.

The Arabic model, Humain-m3, is based on an open-source system from Chinese startup MiniMax. Humain, the state-backed company that commissioned the model, has struck major deals with Nvidia and other U.S. technology companies to build its AI computing capacity.

Saudi Arabia is not alone. From Latin America to Southeast and Central Asia, countries are buying American chips while adopting Chinese open-source models, splitting key AI projects between companies from two AI superpowers. The trend presents a growing complication for Washington’s competition with Beijing. Even countries investing heavily in American AI infrastructure are not necessarily choosing American technology for every layer of the AI stack.

“Many countries around the world, particularly in the Global South, want the best of both worlds,” Kyle Chan, a fellow at the John L. Thornton China Center at the Brookings Institution, told Rest of World. Many countries often do not attach the same security stigma to Chinese technology that Washington does, Chan said. “Ultimately, many countries around the world want to keep their options open and not be too dependent on any single source of technology.”

In August, Brazil announced an investment worth roughly $444 million into AI, which it effectively divided between Chinese and American technologies.

Around $255 million will go toward supercomputing infrastructure in Rio de Janeiro, developed in partnership with China’s HuaweiiHuaweiHuawei is a Chinese technology company focused on mobile phones and telecommunications, and is seen as a poster child for China’s global tech ambitions.READ MORE and iFlytek. The rest, around $189 million, will go to a separate supercomputer that Brazil is currently tendering, but expecting to source from Nvidia.

“The strategy is not to depend on a single company, technology or country,” President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s administration said in a statement, adding that the investments were intended to strengthen Brazil’s sovereignty over its data.

For most countries, technological sovereignty does not mean building an entire AI stack at home, Jesse Marks, a China-Middle East research scholar at the Australian National University, told Rest of World. Competing at the frontier has become prohibitively expensive, leaving governments to decide which technologies they can develop themselves and where they must rely on foreign suppliers.

For Saudi Arabia, it would be a “natural decision” to choose Chinese foundations for sovereign AI models if they perform better on relevant benchmarks, even if doing so carries political consequences with Washington, Marks said.

The U.S., however, has greater leverage in parts of the stack where its technology is harder to replace, such as advanced semiconductors, networking equipment, and sensitive cloud infrastructure. But Washington will struggle with countries that want AI but cannot afford American systems or software, Marks said.

“Outside of the network of American partners who are trusted or can afford it, it’s Chinese AI. It’s open models,” he said.

These technological choices are also becoming intertwined with countries’ broader diplomatic relationships. “AI is one of a number of portfolios that middle powers have to consider when negotiating with a partner like the United States,” Marks said.

Washington has accused Chinese labs of “free-riding” and training their models from frontier American AI models at an “industrial scale.” China, having rejected those accusations, has warned it would retaliate if Washington implements any curbs on Chinese AI companies.

Chinese companies are ramping up efforts to compete with American companies on different layers of the AI stack.

In Egypt, Huawei has bid to build AI data centers for the government, according to a source-based report by Bloomberg, competing against a proposal involving Nvidia. A successful bid would give Chinese companies another foothold in a market where AI infrastructure has so far been dominated by American technology.

Southeast Asia is another region where China-U.S. competition over technological influence is increasingly apparent.

Washington launched the U.S.-ASEAN AI Spark initiative in July, offering financial and technical support to Southeast Asian governments interested in adopting American AI technologies for public-sector use.

Malaysia is considering going in another direction, evaluating Huawei’s Ascend 910C accelerators as the backbone of its sovereign AI initiative, Bloomberg reported.

For now, the two AI superpowers appear to be taking different approaches to building influence abroad.

“China, like any leading power, wants the world to function in a manner that furthers its interests and replicates its own values,” Arindrajit Basu, a doctoral researcher in global governance of emerging technology at Leiden University, told Rest of World. “In the case of the internet and its allied technologies, this is a vision of governance providing a greater preference to the state in maintaining public order and security online. However, China is yet to engage in the naked coercion we have seen from the Trump administration that has reportedly clearly laid out an ultimatum.”

Washington is considering warning against countries trying to align with both U.S.- and China-led AI initiatives. That could put countries already engaging with both sides in a difficult position.

Kazakhstan, for example, has joined the U.S.-led Pax Silica initiative, which aims to build secure AI supply chains spanning semiconductors, compute, and other critical technologies. It has also joined China’s World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization, or WAICO, which focuses on cooperation on AI developmen

analysis.tldr: Global AI rivalry between the U.S. and China does not directly change local Indian prices today, but it shapes how Indian tech firms buy software and hardware.
the_story: Saudi Arabia launched an advanced Arabic AI model called Humain-m3, using technology from Chinese startup MiniMax while simultaneously spending billions on American chips from companies like Nvidia.
Brazil announced a $444 million AI investment in August, splitting it between Chinese firms Huawei and iFlytek for supercomputing infrastructure and American giant Nvidia.
Experts explain that many countries want to avoid depending on a single superpower, mixing cheaper open-source Chinese models with advanced American hardware.
Malaysia is evaluating Huawei’s Ascend 910C accelerators for its sovereign AI initiative, while Egypt sees Huawei competing against Nvidia proposals for government data centers.
Washington holds leverage through hard-to-replace items like advanced semiconductors, but could warn countries against mixing U.S. and Chinese AI initiatives.
analysis.what_happened: Countries around the world are choosing a mix of American hardware and Chinese software for artificial intelligence projects rather than picking just one superpower. Developing nations are doing this to keep their options open, stay within budget, and avoid relying on a single country for critical technology.
analysis.analogy: It is like building a house where you buy the heavy construction tools from one hardware store because they are the strongest, but buy the interior paint and decor from another shop to save money.
why_it_matters_india: Global tech supply chains split further between American hardware and Chinese open-source software.
Indian tech and cloud companies must navigate tighter U.S. export rules and rising geopolitical pressures.
Indian software developers evaluate whether to build on American proprietary systems or open-source Chinese models.
Overall sentiment shifts for Indian technology stocks depending on how global AI hardware rules evolve.

impacts.rationale: Global enterprise demand for AI integration services could shift, though the direct impact of this specific multi-sourcing trend on Indian IT revenues is minimal and mixed.

watch_next: Whether the United States officially implements warnings or restrictions against countries mixing U.S. and Chinese AI technologies
New export rules on American AI chips and computing infrastructure
analysis.caveats: The article focuses broadly on Saudi Arabia, Brazil, and Southeast Asia without directly mentioning Indian policy changes or Indian companies.

history.title: A bank run at the speed of a smartphone
history.what: Silicon Valley Bank lost $42 billion of deposits in a single day and was shut by regulators within about 48 hours of the first sign of trouble — the fastest bank run in history.
history.why: The bank had taken enormous deposits during the technology boom and put them into long-dated government bonds, which carry no credit risk at all. When rates rose sharply in 2022, those bonds lost market value. The holdings were fine if held to maturity and not if it had to sell — and over 90% of its deposits were above the insured limit, so depositors had every reason to run first and ask later. Word spread through group chats.
history.impact: Two more US banks failed within days, and Credit Suisse — unrelated but fragile — was forced into a shotgun merger. Bank shares fell worldwide. Gold rose, as it does whenever people start questioning banks.
history.policy: US regulators guaranteed all deposits at the failed banks, insured or not, and opened a facility letting banks borrow against bonds at face value rather than market value. Supervision of mid-sized banks was tightened.
history.consequence: The rule that only insured deposits are protected was effectively suspended in practice, which stores up its own future problem. It also made interest-rate risk, rather than credit risk, the first thing bank supervisors now ask about.
history.pattern: A government bond has no default risk and plenty of price risk, and that distinction stays invisible until somebody is forced to sell. Meanwhile concentrated, uninsured depositors are the modern queue outside the door — and they move in minutes now, not days.
history.india_echo: Indian deposits are insured only to ₹5 lakh per bank, which is exactly why that limit is flagged under cash on the Asset Classes page. Indian banks hold large government bond portfolios too, though with far stickier retail deposits behind them.
history.watch_for: Banks with depositors concentrated in one industry, and large unrealised losses on bonds held to maturity. Both are disclosed if you look for them.
